power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Over the next decades, the nature of and possibilities for social connection will rapidly evolve with advances in artificial intelligence, mixed-reality technologies, and pervasive digital integration.
Accordingly, psychological science must update how it conceptualizes and measures social connection.
Here, we advance a three-part conceptual framework for understanding social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments.

First, we situate social experiences within a dynamic relational ecosystem-a system of interaction partners and channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that together shape connection.
Second, we conceptualize "alone" and "together" not as binary states but as a gradient shaped by level of physical copresence and communication (shades of aloneness and togetherness).
Third, we conceptualize discrete social interactions as multidimensional, characterized by features such as interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition.

Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades: the decoupling of objective and subjective connection, the erosion of "pure" solitude, the increasing effortfulness and value of in-person interaction, the fragmentation of shared reality, and the growing taken-for-grantedness of connection.
We conclude by discussing methodological and applied implications of this framework.
On the evening of November 2, 1920, families gathered in their living rooms to learn that Warren G. Harding had won the U.S. presidential election.
For the first time, Americans received the same news at the same time through a shared broadcast medium: the radio (Slotten, 2003).

text.text: This first broadcast from a licensed radio station-Pittsburgh's KDKA-signaled a transformation in how people would relate to one another and to the broader social world.

Over the century that followed, successive waves of communication technology have emerged, reshaping possibilities for social life-from the television to landline telephones, from the internet to mobile devices, and from social media to virtual reality and artificially intelligent (AI) chatbots.
Beginning with early forms of written correspondence, social experiences have become more technologically mediated and less tethered to place.

To illustrate, as of 2025, 98% of U.S. adults own cellphones (91% of which are smartphones; Pew Research Center, 2025); internet users globally spend more than six hours online daily (Statista, 2025); over half of new romantic partners meet online (Rosenfeld et al., 2019); and 10% of the global population uses ChatGPT (Chatterji et al., 2025).

text.text: As social inputs become more ambient and ubiquitous-woven into homes, vehicles, workplaces, and even human bodies-people may nearly always be connected, yet they may not necessarily feel connected.
Conversely, people may spend more time physically alone without necessarily feeling alone.
These socio-technological developments raise fundamental questions for psychological science.
What makes an interaction or experience "social" in the first place?
What does it mean to be "alone" or "together" amid constant connectivity?
What becomes of solitude when opportunities for social interaction are virtually impossible to escape?
And finally, how can psychological science help the world navigate changes to social life in ways that promote wellbeing and social connection?

Understanding how to capture and make sense of these changes-and how to help design social environments that promote human flourishing-will be a central challenge for psychological science moving forward.
In this paper, we advance a three-part conceptual framework to help psychological science understand experiences of social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments.

First, we propose viewing social experiences as embedded within dynamic relational ecosystems that include interaction partners, interaction channels, ambient social cues, and broader sociocultural contexts.

Second, within relational ecosystems, individuals occupy a particular shade of aloneness or togetherness, reflecting how physical co-presence and degree of communication combine to shape whether they are alone, together, or somewhere in between in a given moment.
Third, social interactions are characterized by multiple dimensions including (but not limited to) interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition.
Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about the future of social (dis)connection.
We end by discussing methodological and applied implications of this conceptualization.

Our approach draws on historical analysis of prior socio-technological shifts, theoretical extrapolation from current trends, and interdisciplinary research on close relationships, solitude, social connection, human-computer interaction, and well-being.
Our goal is not to predict the future or to speculate about specific technologies that may emerge.

Rather, we aim to articulate some conceptual and methodological considerations to help psychological scientists make sense of social (dis)connection as it evolves-whatever forms future technologies take.
Humans have a fundamental need for social connection and belonging (Baumeister & Leary, 1995; Deci & Ryan, 2000; Dunbar, 1998).

text.text: Accordingly, social life over the next decades is likely to change less in whether we connect, and more in how, when, where, and why we do.
A range of socio-technological developments-including AI, mobile and mixed-reality technologies, and algorithmically mediated platforms-are rapidly restructuring social experiences.
Several long-term shifts are already visible and are likely to accelerate in the decades ahead.
First, social life involves an increasingly expanded set of potential interaction partners.

Although humans have long interacted with nonhuman entities-such as animals, deities, objects, and ancestors (Cerulo, 2009)-AI agents introduce new capabilities and possibilities: they can generate language (e.g., text, speech), respond in ways that are contingent on and tailored to user input, and are available around-the-clock and across physical locations.

text.text: As a result, social experiences-and their psychological consequences-are increasingly structured by the values and incentive systems embedded in the design of technologies.
These developments raise important conceptual questions about what qualifies as a social interaction, and which features of interactions are most consequential for social connection and well-being.

Psychological scientists have developed longstanding, robust theoretical frameworks for understanding interpersonal processes; for example, Interdependence Theory emphasizes how relationships are shaped by patterns of mutual influence between interaction partners (Kelley & Thibaut, 1978), whereas the Intimacy Process Model highlights the central roles of self-disclosure and perceived responsiveness in intimate bonds (Reis & Shaver, 1988).

text.text: These frameworks remain useful for understanding close relationships; however, they were primarily developed to explain face-to-face human relationships and do not explicitly address several features that increasingly vary across contemporary social interactions, including the nature of the interaction partner (human versus nonhuman) and the communication medium (in-person versus online).

Here, following Rodriguez, Trinh, Lieberman, & Schroeder (2026), we conceptualize social interactions as reciprocal, dynamic exchanges during which individuals feel that an entity is attending to or engaging with them in ways that are contingent on their input.

text.text: Under this definition, social interactions can involve both human and nonhuman interaction partners, including AI chatbots, virtual assistants, animals, and deities (Archer, 1997; Chan et al., 2019; Inzlicht et al., 2024; Telari et al., 2026).

text.text: We distinguish social interactions from the social experiences, which are broader experiences involving social information, representations, or stimuli that evoke shared meaning but do not require reciprocal exchange.

Such experiences may arise in the absence of direct social interaction, such as in the case of consuming traditional mass media (e.g., newspaper, radio, television, books), listening to music, or visiting a public space (e.g., public park, church, museum).
These structural shifts in social life change not only how and with whom we interact, but the conditions under which social connection unfolds in the first place.
Social experiences are increasingly distributed across diverse interaction partners, locations, channels, and algorithmic systems that influence attention and engagement.

As a result, social connection is increasingly difficult to understand as a series of discrete, bounded interactions between humans alone, urging us to rethink how we conceptualize and measure social connection.
Here, we propose viewing individuals as situated within dynamic relational ecosystems.

Drawing inspiration from classic perspectives emphasizing that human behavior is fundamentally embedded within broader social relations (Granovetter, 1985) and ecological systems (Bronfenbrenner, 1979), we define relational ecosystems as the set of interaction partners, interaction channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that shape an individual's social environment at any given moment in time (see Fig. 1).

text.text: Interaction partners are the entities with which one is actively interacting, such as friends, pets, AI chatbots, deities, and virtual avatars.
Interaction channels are the pathways through which social interaction occurs, including (but not limited to) face-to-face, texting, audio or video call, social media, and virtual reality.

Ambient social cues are environmental features that signal the presence or possibility of social connection without involving direct interaction, including nearby conversations, music, people, animals, digital notifications, and technological devices.
Relational ecosystems also include broader sociocultural contexts.

Social norms, belief systems, expectations, and institutions, among other factors, shape how individuals interpret and engage with their social environments-for example, whether time alone is valued or stigmatized (Rodriguez et al., 2025; Rodriguez, Baldwin, et al., in press), the extent to which AI chatbots are adopted and how they are perceived (Folk et al., 2025; Scherr et al., 2025), and how socially embedded individuals are in the first place (Campos & Kim, 2017; Markus & Kitayama, 1991).

text.text: As a result, the same objective social interactions may afford belonging and a felt sense of connection for some individuals while leaving others feeling disconnected, depending on how they align with culturally-shaped norms and expectations.

To be clear, humans have always lived within relational ecosystems.

For millennia and across diverse cultures, people have interacted and formed relationships with both human and nonhuman entities, including animals, deities, ancestors, natural organisms (e.g., trees), and technological devices (Cerulo, 2009; Epley et al., 2008; Kohn, 2013; Waytz, 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2026; Wormley et al., 2025).

text.text: They have interacted with others via different channels (e.g., letters) and within organized social structures (e.g., church).

Nevertheless, a key feature that distinguishes contemporary (and future) relational ecosystems from previous ones is that they afford 24/7 accessibility to social interaction, simulated reciprocity through responsive artificial agents that perform tasks that historically required human intelligence, algorithmic curation of socially-relevant information, and personalization at scale.
These features do not merely increase the quantity of potential social interactions; they also alter their structure and psychological meaning.
As such, we as psychological scientists need to embrace this complexity and develop more sophisticated and layered frameworks if we want to adequately capture modern (and future) social experiences.
Within relational ecosystems, individuals can engage in multiple forms of social interaction-human and nonhuman, online and offline-simultaneously or in close succession (Campbell et al., 2026).

text.text: These dynamics may influence one another in complex ways to affect subjective social connection and psychological well-being.
Engagement in one modality may displace or complement others, spill over across contexts, and recalibrate expectations for responsiveness.

For example, attending to one's phone during an in-person interaction (i.e., phubbing) can undermine the quality of that interaction, illustrating how engagement in one domain directly disrupts another (McDaniel, & Coyne, 2016; Vanden Abeele, 2020).

text.text: In addition, recent interaction with a sycophantic AI chatbot may render a subsequent disagreement with a romantic partner more painful and frustrating.

Understanding these dynamics requires moving beyond models that treat interactions as isolated events and toward frameworks that capture how social experiences are distributed across layered, continuously evolving environments.
Historically, physical aloneness implied the absence of human interaction: to be alone was to be objectively disconnected from other people.
In contemporary environments, however, people are frequently socially connected even when physically alone.
Accordingly, objective experiences of being "alone" versus "together" increasingly defy binary classification, which complicates how researchers conceptualize and operationalize these constructs.
This tension is most clearly reflected in contemporary research on solitude.

Some scholars define solitude as physical aloneness, whereas others view it as social aloneness, or "noncommunication" (Campbell & Ross, 2022; Coplan et al., 2022; Nguyen & Rodriguez, 2024; Rodriguez et al., 2025).

text.text: Yet each of these definitions faces growing limitations.
What type of presence is required for someone to no longer be considered physically "alone"-are you "alone" when seated on a park bench 20 feet from a stranger?
Or when petting a dog or holding a newborn baby (Nguyen et al., 2026)?

text.text: Or when interacting with avatars in virtual reality?
And what even is "noncommunication" in a world of constant connectivity increasingly populated by potential human and nonhuman interaction partners?
To accommodate these increasingly complex forms of social experience, we propose conceptualizing being "alone" versus "together" as a gradient rather than mutually exclusive states (see Fig. 2).

text.text: Specifically, we draw on two commonly used conceptualizations of solitudephysical aloneness and noncommunication-to construct this two-dimensional framework.

The examples shown in the figure are intended to demonstrate how different configurations of physical co-presence and communication may situate experiences within this conceptual space.
They do not imply that any activity occupies one fixed position.

In practice, the same experience (e.g., "texting someone") may shift across the space depending on contextual factors such as whether communication is synchronous or asynchronous, as well as physical proximity to others.

An individual's placement within this two-dimensional space at a particular moment in time is shaped by their relational ecosystem-namely, the configuration of ongoing social interactions and ambient social cues at a given moment.
Importantly, a given position in this space may reflect not a single discrete interaction, but the combined influence of multiple simultaneous or rapidly shifting layers of social experience.

One may be, for example, physically alone while virtually interacting with humans or nonhuman agents; physically co-present with other humans but socially disengaged; physically surrounded by others while immersed in virtual reality; or physically alone and not interacting with any social entity at all (i.e., "pure" solitude).

These configurations-which may only become more complex as new digital communication tools, interaction partners, and forms of ambient social cues emerge (Boase, 2025)-reflect qualitatively different shades of aloneness and togetherness that may give rise to distinct subjective psychological experiences.

text.text: Across time, individuals may continuously shift between different shades of aloneness and togetherness as their patterns of communication and physical co-presence change.

Notably, some positions in this gradient may reflect the absence of social interaction, whereas others may reflect one or multiple social interactions occurring simultaneously or in close succession within a particular context.

Understanding social experience thus requires not only mapping where a person is situated within this experiential gradient, but also considering whether that position includes social interaction and, when it does, examining the nature, quality, and meaning of such interactions.
To better distinguish between increasingly heterogeneous kinds of social interactions, one useful approach is to conceptualize social interactions as multidimensional.

Each social interaction can be characterized by a set of features including (but not limited to) interaction partner (e.g., human to nonhuman), relationship type (e.g., least close [e.g., stranger] to closest [e.g., romantic partner]), medium (offline to online), temporality (e.g., synchronous to asynchronous), engagement (e.g., passive to active), and volition (e.g., low [involuntary] to high [deliberately chosen]).

This multidimensional approach builds on ample existing work in psychology and related fields (e.g., communication) that has distinguished between different types of social engagement.

For example, researchers have tested the effects of active versus passive social media use (Godard & Holtzman, 2024), synchronous versus asynchronous text message interactions (Park & Sundar, 2015), spoken versus written disagreements (Bevis et al., 2026), and AI versus human interactions (Li et al., 2026).

text.text: What is increasingly needed, however, is a framework that integrates across these dimensions.

Indeed, two people may spend the same amount of time engaged in social interactions on a given day, but those interactions may differ dramatically in their temporality, communication medium, and type(s) of interaction partners.
Importantly, we do not propose these dimensions as an exhaustive taxonomy of social interaction.
Rather, we offer them as a heuristic framework for guiding future theory development, measurement, and empirical work.

In so doing, this framework encourages researchers to move beyond relying solely on the frequency or duration of social interactions and instead characterize interactions according to multiple features.

It also suggests new opportunities for experimental research by allowing investigators to isolate specific interaction characteristics and examine their independent and interactive effects on social connection and well-being.
Among the dimensions listed, volition may be particularly consequential moving forward.
The future of social (dis)connection may be characterized by two seemingly contradictory trends.
On one hand, some forms of social interaction may require greater intentionality than in the past.

Historically, social interaction was often embedded within daily life: people often lived in larger households, worked alongside others, participated in religious institutions, and encountered the same individuals repeatedly within their communities (Dunbar, 1998; Putnam, 2000).

text.text: As rates of living alone continue to increase across many global regions (Rodriguez, Baldwin, et al., in press), remote work expands, and daily activities become increasingly digitized (e.g., food delivery, shopping, banking, and dating), opportunities for spontaneous (or routine) face-to-face interaction have declined (Pfeifer & Mehl, 2026).

text.text: As a result, initiating and maintaining social relationships may increasingly require deliberate effort.
On the other hand, future social interactions may be characterized by reduced volition in other ways.

As engagement with digital technologies becomes increasingly habitual, people are routinely exposed to social information and opportunities for social interaction through push notifications, autoplay features, and algorithmically curated feeds-even when they are not intentionally seeking them out (Bayer et al., 2016 (Bayer et al., , 2022)).

text.text: In line with this idea, research on digital disconnection shows that control over attention and social availability has become increasingly valued (Vanden Abeele et al., 2024), and perceived control over media use predicts whether digital interactions are experienced as detrimental to well-being (Lee & Hancock, 2024).

text.text: Accordingly, a central question for future research is the extent to which social interactions are self-initiated, controllable, and aligned with individuals' goals and needs.

Taken together, relational ecosystems (Fig. 1) define the broader social environment in which individuals are embedded at a given moment in time, including the full set of interaction partners, interaction channels, ambient social cues, and broader sociocultural contexts.

text.text: At a more granular level, these configurations are shaped by the presence (or absence) of social interactions (Fig. 3), which are multidimensional.

text.text: In all, this conceptual framework distinguishes between three complementary levels of analysis: the relational ecosystem (the broader social environment), shade of aloneness or togetherness (momentary experiential states), and social interactions (discrete social exchanges).
Although this framework expands how psychological science can conceptualize and measure the structure of social life, mapping objective social environments is only part of the picture.
A central challenge remains: understanding how individuals subjectively experience and interpret their social environments.
Psychological scientists have long distinguished between objective and subjective indicators of social connection (Baek et al., 2025; Perlman & Peplau, 1981).
text.formatted: Psychological scientists have long distinguished between objective and subjective indicators of social connection <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baek et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Perlman & Peplau, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: It is wellestablished that objective social connection (e.g., frequency of interaction, social network size, time spent with others) does not reliably map onto subjective experience (e.g., how connected people feel).
One can be surrounded by-or actively interacting with-others and still feel lonely (Coyle & Dugan, 2012; Danvers et al., 2023; Hawkley & Cacioppo, 2010; Perlman & Peplau, 1981; Stavrova & Ren, 2023).

text.text: Accordingly, capturing subjective connection-the felt sense of closeness, belonging, or understanding-is essential.
In the future, novel tools, such as passive neurobiological sensors, may increasingly allow researchers to index how (dis)connected people feel.
But for now, subjective connection continues to be best assessed through self-report.
The relationship between objective and subjective connection is, and will likely continue to be, systematically shaped by individual differences.

For example, prior work demonstrates that people who are more prone to anthropomorphize are more likely to feel socially connected to AI chatbots (Folk et al., 2025); socially anxious individuals are more likely to feel lonely when around others (Lim et al., 2016); people who are less trusting of humans are more trusting of AI agents (Molina & Sundar, 2024); those who view being alone as a beneficial experience are more likely to reap its psychological benefits (Rodriguez et al., 2020 (Rodriguez et al., , 2023 (Rodriguez et al., , 2025)); and people vary widely in whether they perceive social media platforms as socially connective (Rhee et al., 2021; Rodriguez, Motyl, & Schroeder, 2026).

text.text: Further, individual differences in familiarity with and access to social technologies, as well as digital literacy, may also shape which forms of connection are available or psychologically meaningful (Hargittai, 2003; van Dijk, 2006).

text.text: Accordingly, as social interaction becomes more technologically mediated-and increasingly involves diverse AI agents without human consciousness-the same social environments may be experienced as connective and rewarding for some yet superficial or even aversive for others.

This variability highlights the continued importance of understanding social connection not only in terms of objective structures, but also through the subjective lenses that color how it is experienced.
Building on our conceptual framework, we propose five theoretically grounded, testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades.

As relational ecosystems afford more continuous and diverse forms of social interaction, objective indicators of social connection-such as frequency of in-person interactions, social network size, or living arrangements-may become progressively weak predictors of subjective connection.
In many cases, individuals may be persistently "connected" in an objective sense while feeling lonely and socially unfulfilled.

As opportunities for interaction become more ubiquitous across physical, digital, and hybrid environments, assessing both objective and subjective forms of connection will become even more important, as these constructs may become increasingly decoupled and may predict different psychological and health outcomes.
Prediction 2.
The Erosion of Pure Solitude.

As possibilities for social interaction expand and become less tethered to physical space, sustained periods of "pure solitude" (both physical aloneness and noncommunication; see Fig. 2) will grow increasingly rare and more difficult to achieve.

text.text: This erosion of pure solitude, in which opportunities to connect crowd out opportunities to be alone, may have important consequences.

Philosophers like Kierkegaard and Nietzsche regarded separation from social influence as essential for authenticity and moral clarity, and research has documented several psychological functions of solitude including emotion regulation, self-reflection, and autonomy (Rodriguez & Campbell, 2025; Nguyen et al., 2018; Weinstein et al., 2021).

text.text: If increasingly digital relational ecosystems constrain this inwardness, individuals may face not only the potential costs of reduced face-to-face interaction (Pfeifer & Mehl, 2026), but also the psychological costs of never truly being alone.

text.text: Navigating close human relationships is not an easy endeavor; it requires coordination, compromise, and responsiveness to others' needs (Finkel et al., 2017; Kelley & Thibaut, 1978).

text.text: Although humans have historically engaged with lower-demand forms of social connection (e.g., pets, media figures, or casual social ties), AI chatbots are rapidly increasing the accessibility and sophistication of such lower-cost alternatives.
As these highly responsive, customizable, and relatively frictionless interactions become more common, human interaction will be experienced as comparatively more demanding (Perry, 2026).

text.text: Prediction 4.
The Increased Fragmentation of Shared Reality.
Humans are motivated to create a sense of shared reality with others (Echterhoff et al., 2009; Higgins et al., 2021).

text.text: Historically, people experienced relatively shared social environments-such as geographicallybounded communities and overlapping social networks (Dunbar, 1998)-which facilitated this construction of shared reality.

text.text: However, as previously discussed, contemporary relational ecosystems differ in an important way: algorithmically curated environments and AI-mediated interactions enable highly individualized streams of information (Matz et al., 2017).

text.text: As a result, individuals may inhabit increasingly personalized social worlds, with potentially reduced overlap in the content they consume or the interaction partners they engage with, human and AI alike (Sunstein, 2018).

text.text: This is likely to weaken people's sense of shared reality and widen the divergence in their beliefs and lived experiences, with potentially important downstream implications for economic, political, and health outcomes (e.g., political polarization, misinformation, health behavior adoption; Levy & Razin, 2019; Van Bavel et al., 2024).

text.text: Prediction 5.
The Taken-for-Grantedness of Social Connection.

As opportunities for social interaction become more ubiquitous, the around-the-clock availability and responsiveness of interaction partners (whether human or nonhuman) may come to be taken for granted-that is, experienced as default conditions rather than notable features of social life.

In other words, as objective connectivity becomes even more normalized, people may become less likely to consciously appreciate connection when it occurs and more likely to notice, react to, or feel frustrated by its absence when expected responsiveness is disrupted.

This pattern has clear precedent: earlier communication technologies, such as timekeeping and mobile telephony, initially felt novel and remarkable but gradually became taken for granted once they were reliably embedded in everyday routines (Ling, 2012 (Ling, , 2014;; Ross & Campbell, 2021).

text.text: As the internet becomes "like oxygen," in that it is omnipresent and difficult to disengage from (Stansberry et al., 2019), social norms surrounding constant connectivity may further intensify (Bayer et al., 2016).

text.text: Over time, this shift may amplify the psychological toll of disconnection.
What do these predictions suggest for the future of social (dis)connection?
To be sure, humans are highly adaptable and have long adjusted to shifting social and technological environments (Henrich, 2015; Richerson & Boyd, 2004).
text.formatted: To be sure, humans are highly adaptable and have long adjusted to shifting social and technological environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Henrich, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Richerson & Boyd, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, adaptation alone does not always guarantee optimal outcomes.
As relational ecosystems continue to evolve, individuals may adapt to conditions that do not necessarily support subjective connection or well-being.
Importantly, these trajectories are not deterministic: they are shaped by human decisions, institutional structures (e.g., policy), and technological design.

Understanding why and in what ways social connection is changing-as well as how it can be deliberately shaped in ways that promote well-being-will therefore be a central task for psychological science moving forward.
Below, we outline some methodological and applied considerations for meeting this challenge.
As relational ecosystems become more densely populated and complex, our measurement tools must evolve accordingly.
As previously noted, contemporary approaches to capturing subjective social connection via self-report remain useful.
However, approaches to measuring objective social connection are increasingly limited.

For example, assessing the number of inperson interactions does not fully capture the range of social experiences people have, and capturing time spent on social media collapses across theoretically meaningful dimensions (e.g., engagement, temporality) and is too coarse to meaningfully assess online social experiences (Maheux et al., 2025; Valkenburg, 2022).

text.text: Moreover, reliance on self-reported digital media use-which is only modestly correlated with objectively logged use-raises validity concerns (Parry et al., 2021).

text.text: Fortunately, the very technologies reshaping social life also offer novel and promising tools for studying it.

Mobile sensing-the use of digital devices (e.g., smartphones, wearables, smart home devices) to passively collect data about people's behavior, context, and physiology-enables ecologically valid assessments of social life as it unfolds in real time (Harari & Gosling, 2023; Gordon et al., 2025; Gordon & Mendes, 2021).

text.text: New data collection paradigms also offer novel ways of capturing how people interact with technology.
One example is Screenomics, the moment-by-moment account of on-screen content (Ram et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One example is Screenomics, the moment-by-moment account of on-screen content <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Ram et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: When paired with self-report to capture subjective experiences of social connection, these approaches allow researchers to test how different dimensions of objective socio-technological conditions map onto subjective connection.

As these digital methods often originate outside of psychology (e.g., Communication, Computer Science), they underscore the importance of psychological scientists reaching beyond their own paradigms and collaborating across disciplines to better understand these matters.
Beyond documenting the evolution of social (dis)connection over the next decades psychological science is uniquely positioned to help inform it.

As relational ecosystems become increasingly influenced by technological advancements, social connection will be influenced not only by individual preferences and choices, but also by the social norms, incentives, and infrastructures that guide those choices (i.e., the sociocultural context).

This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for psychological scientists-who have deep insights into social connection-to inform how these relational ecosystems are built (e.g., Zhao, 2026).
text.formatted: This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for psychological scientists-who have deep insights into social connection-to inform how these relational ecosystems are built (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Zhao, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, individuals' preferences and goals are themselves shaped by social norms and design choices.

As a result, what people want-for example, relying on AI for emotional support instead of other humans because it feels less effortful-may not always align with what supports their health and well-being.
Accordingly, interventions may need to extend beyond supporting individual agency to also target the social and structural conditions that shape whether and how connection is pursued.

These efforts may include designing culturally sensitive environments (Markus et al., 2025) that nudge individuals toward beneficial forms of social connection or reduce barriers to engaging in them in the first place.
text.formatted: These efforts may include designing culturally sensitive environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Markus et al., 2025)</ref> that nudge individuals toward beneficial forms of social connection or reduce barriers to engaging in them in the first place.

text.text: At the same time, efforts to shape the future of social connection must grapple with competing incentives across scientific, commercial, and policy domains.

Technology companies are often driven by engagement-based business models that may pose risks to users (Kang et al., 2026; Haidt & Rausch, 2026), and partnerships between researchers and industry carry welldocumented risks-including reinforcing existing industry norms, limiting transparency, or serving reputational rather than substantive goals (Mitroff & Sharpe, 2017).

text.text: Achieving meaningful change will therefore require not only rigorous theoretical and empirical work, but also institutional conditions that support independence, accountability, and high-integrity collaborations.
In this context, policy represents a critical lever for shaping the future of social (dis)connection (Krems & Kaufman, 2026; Holt-Lunstad, 2023).

text.text: Decisions about platform design, data governance, transparency, and accountability will very likely shape how social connection unfolds at scale.
Ideally, policy can help better align industry incentives with the public good, so that promoting social connection is not perpetually in tension with profit.

For example, regulation could play a constructive role here by requiring greater transparency-such as mandating that digital platforms share long-term and real-time data with independent researchers to assess the benefits and harms of digital technologies for social connection (Office of the U.S. Surgeon General, 2023a, 2023b).
Furthermore, waiting for definitive causal evidence before informing policy may not be feasible-and may, in practice, cede default governance to profit-driven systems (Orben, 2020; Richtel, 2023).

text.text: A more reasonable and pragmatic approach is to act on the best available evidence while committing to ongoing evaluation, transparency about uncertainty, and course correction as new evidence emerges (Murthy, 2024).

text.text: With this approach, public trust in science is critical, as is clear science communication.
The stakes are high.

text.text: Importantly, these trajectories are not inevitable.

Rather than adopting a technologically deterministic view, we emphasize that the future of social (dis)connection can be shaped by scientific, societal, and policy choices, just as they can by technological design.
How future relational ecosystems are constructed, regulated, and used can shape the extent to which they support or undermine human connection and well-being.
The most consequential social psychological experiments of the next century will not take place in a laboratory.
They will unfold in the increasingly complex and dynamic relational ecosystems through which people live, relate to one another, and participate in social life.
As the nature of and possibilities for social connection evolve, theoretical frameworks, definitions, and methodological approaches must evolve alongside them.

Therefore, the challenge ahead is not simply to document how social life changes, but to ensure that our tools keep pace with transformations that may redefine the very meaning of social (dis)connection.
